newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Defector's comments stir fears in S.Korea.
newsitem.headline: Defector's comments stir fears in S.Korea.

text.p: Stunning revelations reported to have been made by a high-ranking North Korean defector sparked security fears and political controversy in South Korea on Friday.
"Fifty thousand spies in South Korea," a banner headline in the Munhwa Ilbo newspaper quoted defector Hwang Jang-yop as telling a senior South Korean official.

Hwang, a powerful secretary of Stalinist North Korea's ruling Workers' Party who turned up on Wednesday at the South Korean embassy compound in Beijing, told the Seoul official in Beijing last August he wanted to seek political asylum, the paper said.
"Secretary Hwang said at that time more than 50,000 North Korean spies were operating in the South," the official was quoted as saying.
The ruling New Korea Party, referring to another media report on spy infiltration, urged intelligence authorities to launch a thorough search for North Korean moles in the South.
"We should take seriously remarks made by defector Hwang Jang-yop that North Koreans are planted deep in the South Korean power structure," party spokesman Kim Chul said.

"We cannot help but take Hwang's words more seriously because our intelligence organisation has compiled statistics that there are 40,000 pro-North Korean forces in our society although they are not spies," he said in a statement.

The leading Chosun Ilbo newspaper's version said Hwang's warning about North Korean moles was made to a South Korean businessman who often received the senior North Korean official's notes through one of his aides.
Government officials have not confirmed or denied the newspaper reports, but the ruling party's statement added to their weight.

The main opposition National Congress for New Politics attacked the government for leaving grave questions unanswered and voiced fears it might be using the defection drama to divert public attention away from a political crisis over a loan scandal that is eating into President Kim Young-sam's credibility.
"If what Hwang said is true, our national security is in tatters," National Congress lawmaker Yoo Jong-pil said.
Hwang, ideological chief of the tottering communist regime, is ranked 24th in the North's hierarchy and is the highest Pyongyang official to seek political asylum in South Korea.
"The government appears to be using the defection in a bid to overcome its political difficulties," said National Congress spokeswoman Park Sun-suck.
A corruption scandal swirling around massive loans to a failed steelmaker has badly hurt President Kim's anti-graft reform campaign by implicating close associates.
Kim had already been smarting from a humiliating climbdown over a controversial labour law, which he sent back to parliament for review after nearly a month of labour strikes against the law.
Opposition members said some of Hwang's remarks echoed hardline policies of the Seoul government.
The remarks supported the government's passage of the labour law, which made it easier for companies to sack workers, and another controversial bill that boosts the power of its intelligence body.

Hwang also urged South Korea to stop providing aid to Pyongyang and to allow the already huge economic gap between the two Koreas to widen, saying that was the only way to expedite reunification of the Korean peninsula, split since the end of World War Two.

The Chosun Ilbo, which often publishes leaks by government officials, said one of its reporters had obtained several of Hwang's letters since late last year through the businessmen. The businessmen asked the reporter not to publish them until the planned defection took place.
In one of the letters revealed on Friday, Hwang said he decided to defect to South Korea last May when Pyongyang's leadership started criticising his socialist ideology.

In a signed note released by the Seoul government on Thursday, Hwang attacked those in the North who continue to treat South Korea as the enemy and threaten to turn it into a "sea of fire" while proposing national unification.
